title: Implement vector search with Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.q: Which pgvector operator calculates cosine distance?

options.why: <-> is L2 (Euclidean) distance.
<#> is negative inner product.
Correct. <=> is cosine distance.
@> is the JSONB containment operator.

questions.hint: pgvector has three distance operators. Cosine is the one with an equals sign.
questions.explain: <-> L2, <=> cosine, <#> negative inner product.

questions.q: You enable vector search on an Azure Database for PostgreSQL database. Which command adds pgvector?

options.text: az postgres flexible-server parameter set --name vector.enabled
options.why: Learn enables pgvector with CREATE EXTENSION.

options.text: CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
options.why: Correct. The extension name is vector.

options.text: ALTER DATABASE SET vector = on;
options.why: Extensions aren't enabled with a database setting like this.

options.text: CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pgvector_search;
options.why: That isn't the extension's name.

questions.hint: Extensions are added with a CREATE statement, and the extension's name is short.
questions.explain: Run CREATE EXTENSION with a role such as azure_pg_admin.

questions.q: Inserts into `embedding vector(1536)` fail after the team switched to a sentence transformer model. What's the likely cause?

options.text: Sentence transformer vectors need the <#> operator to insert
options.why: Operators are for queries, not inserts.

options.text: Its 384-dimension output doesn't match vector(1536)
options.why: Correct. Sentence transformers typically output 384 dimensions; mismatched counts cause insert errors.

options.text: pgvector needs a halfvec column for non-OpenAI models
options.why: halfvec is about precision, not model vendors.

options.text: The extension has to be re-created after any model change
options.why: The extension doesn't need re-creating.

questions.hint: vector(n) must match the model's output size.
questions.explain: vector(n) must match the model's output dimension.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A query uses `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10` on a vector(1536) column.

rows.text: Rows with smaller values are more similar to the query.
A cosine distance of 2 means the vectors point in opposite directions.
rows.why: Cosine distance ranges from 0 (identical direction) to 2 (opposite).

rows.text: Storing the column as halfvec(1536) would double the storage.
The <#> operator returns cosine similarity, where larger is better.
rows.why: <#> is negative inner product; like the other operators, smaller is better.

questions.hint: For distances, smaller means closer. Cosine distance runs from 0 to 2. halfvec saves space.
questions.explain: pgvector distances: smaller is closer; vector type ≈ 4 bytes per dimension.

questions.q: A model produces sparse embeddings with about 3,000 non-zero values out of 30,000 dimensions, and you want an HNSW index. What should you know?

options.text: sparsevec can't be indexed at all, so store it as vector(30000)
options.why: sparsevec can be indexed within the limit.

options.text: HNSW handles any number of non-zero elements on sparsevec
options.why: There's a 1,000 non-zero element limit.

options.text: HNSW on sparsevec allows up to 1,000 non-zero elements
options.why: Correct. Learn notes the 1,000 non-zero element limit for HNSW on sparsevec.

options.text: halfvec is required for sparse embeddings above 1,000 values
options.why: halfvec is for dense half-precision vectors.

questions.hint: HNSW on sparse vectors has a limit on non-zero elements.
questions.explain: sparsevec stores only non-zero values; HNSW supports up to 1,000 of them.

questions.q: Match each pgvector operator to the distance it calculates.

items.why: <-> is L2 (Euclidean) distance, used with vector_l2_ops.
<=> is cosine distance, used with vector_cosine_ops.
<#> is negative inner product, used with vector_ip_ops for maximum inner product search.

questions.hint: One operator has a hash mark, one has an equals sign, and one has a dash.
questions.explain: pgvector operators: <-> L2 distance, <=> cosine distance, <#> negative inner product. For all three, smaller results mean closer vectors.

questions.q: Queries use the <=> operator. Which operator class should the HNSW index use?

options.text: gin_trgm_ops
options.why: That's for trigram text search, not vectors.

options.text: vector_l2_ops
options.why: vector_l2_ops matches <->.

options.text: vector_cosine_ops
options.why: Correct. vector_cosine_ops matches <=>.

options.text: vector_ip_ops
options.why: vector_ip_ops matches <#>.

questions.hint: The operator class must match the operator used in queries.
questions.explain: Operator class and query operator must match, or PostgreSQL falls back to a sequential scan.

questions.q: You create an IVFFlat index on a new, empty table and then load 500,000 vectors. Search results are poor. Why?

options.text: IVFFlat can't index more than 100,000 vectors
options.why: Learn gives no such limit.

options.text: IVFFlat needs existing data to train its clusters
options.why: Correct. An IVFFlat index created on an empty table isn't usable; load data first.

options.text: IVFFlat has to be created with CONCURRENTLY
options.why: CONCURRENTLY avoids blocking; it doesn't fix untrained clusters.

options.text: IVFFlat requires the vector_ip_ops operator class
options.why: Any matching operator class works.

questions.hint: IVFFlat builds its clusters from data that already exists.
questions.explain: Load data, then create IVFFlat. HNSW, by contrast, can start on an empty table.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A product search app uses HNSW with default settings.

rows.text: The default number of connections per node (m) is 16.
Raising ef_search to 100–200 typically lowers recall.

questions.hint: HNSW defaults: 16 connections per node and a search list of 40. A bigger search list raises recall.
questions.explain: m and ef_construction shape the graph; ef_search sets query-time width.

questions.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Seq Scan for `SELECT id FROM documents ORDER BY embedding <-> $1`, although an HNSW index with vector_l2_ops exists on a large table. What is most likely missing?

options.text: A LIMIT clause on the query
options.why: Correct. Vector indexes are most effective with ORDER BY and LIMIT; Learn lists the missing LIMIT as a cause of Seq Scan.

options.text: A GIN index on the content column
options.why: GIN indexes help full-text search, not vector ordering.

options.text: An IVFFlat index as well
options.why: A second index type isn't needed.

options.text: A halfvec column type
options.why: The data type isn't the cause here.

questions.hint: The planner uses a vector index only for ORDER BY distance with a LIMIT.
questions.explain: Check operator class, index validity, table size and the LIMIT clause when you see Seq Scan.

questions.q: A query asks for `LIMIT 100` results from an HNSW index while `hnsw.ef_search` is still at its default. What should you change?

options.text: Lower hnsw.ef_search to 20 for speed
options.why: Lower values trade recall for speed and are still below the LIMIT.

options.text: Rebuild the index with a larger m
options.why: m is a build-time parameter; ef_search is the query-time setting here.

options.text: Raise hnsw.ef_search to at least 100
options.why: Correct. ef_search should be at least as large as the number of results you request; the default is 40.

options.text: Switch the operator class to vector_ip_ops
options.why: The operator class must match the query operator; it isn't the issue.

questions.hint: ef_search should be at least the number of results you ask for.
questions.explain: Set ef_search per session with SET hnsw.ef_search = …; it should be at least the LIMIT.

questions.q: A 50-million-row embeddings table needs searches under 100 ms, and the team can accept that a few true nearest neighbors are occasionally missed. What fits?

options.text: No index, with LIMIT 10 to keep the scan short
options.why: Without an index, the database still compares every row before sorting.

options.text: An exact sequential scan with a larger server
options.why: An exact scan computes 50 million distances per query, far too slow for 100 ms.

options.text: An approximate nearest-neighbor index such as HNSW
options.why: Correct. ANN search trades perfect accuracy for dramatic speed, measured as recall.

options.text: A B-tree index on the embedding column
options.why: B-tree indexes don't support nearest-neighbor distance search.

questions.hint: The team accepts "occasionally missed". Which kind of index trades a little accuracy for speed?
questions.explain: Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes examine only a subset of vectors, trading perfect accuracy for speed. Recall measures how many true nearest neighbors appear in the results.

questions.q: An IVFFlat index has lists = 100. You're choosing a starting value for ivfflat.probes. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Set probes to 1 so that queries stay as fast as possible
options.why: One probe is fast but searches the fewest clusters, which can hurt recall. Learn's starting point is sqrt(lists).

options.text: Set probes equal to lists divided by 2, then never change it
options.why: Learn gives sqrt(lists) as the starting point, and says to adjust it for your recall and latency needs.

options.text: Set probes to 100 so that every cluster is searched
options.why: That searches everything, which removes the index's speed benefit.

options.text: Start at 10, the square root of lists, then tune for recall and latency
options.why: Correct. Start with probes = sqrt(lists) and adjust based on your recall and latency needs.

questions.hint: Learn gives a square-root rule of thumb.
questions.explain: probes controls how many clusters are searched at query time. Higher values improve recall but increase latency. Start with probes = sqrt(lists), set per session with SET ivfflat.probes.

questions.q: You must rebuild a vector index on a production table without blocking queries. What should you use?

options.text: VACUUM FULL documents to rebuild storage
options.why: VACUUM FULL reclaims space and locks the table; it doesn't rebuild the vector index structure.

options.text: DROP INDEX first, then CREATE INDEX again
options.why: Dropping first leaves queries without an index.

options.text: REINDEX INDEX on the existing vector index
options.why: REINDEX blocks writes during the rebuild.

options.text: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, then swap names
options.why: Correct. Build concurrently, verify, drop the old index and rename.

questions.hint: Build a replacement without blocking, then swap names.
questions.explain: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY takes longer but keeps serving requests.

questions.q: You're migrating from a 1,536-dimension model to a 3,072-dimension model with no downtime. Put the parallel-column steps in order.
steps: Add a new column, embedding_v2 vector(3072)
Create an HNSW index on embedding_v2
Switch queries to embedding_v2 after comparing results
Drop the old column and index, then rename the new ones
questions.hint: Add the new column and its index, fill it, switch, then clean up.
questions.explain: Parallel columns let you validate the new model and roll back if it underperforms.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. Editors update document text hundreds of times an hour, and embeddings are regenerated in the same transaction.

rows.text: Marking rows embedding_stale = TRUE and re-embedding in batches would lower content update latency.
rows.why: Batching decouples content updates from embedding generation.

rows.text: Synchronous re-embedding in the same transaction is Learn's advice for frequent edits.
rows.why: For frequent changes, Learn recommends async batch processing with a stale flag.

rows.text: PostgreSQL reclaims disk space immediately when a row is updated.
rows.why: MVCC keeps old row versions until VACUUM reclaims them.

rows.text: VACUUM FULL is the non-locking option for busy tables.
rows.why: VACUUM FULL locks the table; standard VACUUM runs concurrently.

questions.hint: For frequent edits, mark rows stale and re-embed in batches.
questions.explain: For frequent updates: stale flags, batch re-embedding, and tuned autovacuum.

questions.q: A table will hold 1 million rows with `vector(1536)` embeddings. Roughly how much storage does the vector column alone need, before any index?

options.text: About 6 GB
options.why: Correct. 1,536 dimensions × 4 bytes ≈ 6 KB per row, so about 6 GB for a million rows.

options.text: About 1.5 GB
options.why: That's the size for 384-dimension vectors.

options.text: About 60 GB
options.why: That's ten times too large.

options.text: About 12 GB
options.why: That's the size for 3,072-dimension vectors.

questions.hint: Each float32 element is 4 bytes. Multiply by dimensions and rows.
questions.explain: Vector column storage ≈ dimensions × 4 bytes × rows; indexes add more on top.

questions.q: You loaded embeddings from a new document domain, adding about 35% more rows. Search latency is up, and users say results are less relevant. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Drop the index and rely on exact scans
options.why: Exact scans are too slow at this size.

options.text: Change the operator class to vector_ip_ops
options.why: The operator class must match the query operator. Changing it doesn't fix a stale structure.

options.text: Lower hnsw.ef_search to make queries faster
options.why: That lowers recall further, which makes relevance worse.

options.text: Rebuild the vector index, for example with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
options.why: Correct. Adding more than 20–30% new data, especially from a new domain, often warrants rebuilding the ANN index.

questions.hint: ANN indexes are shaped by the data they were built on. A lot of new data changes that.
questions.explain: ANN indexes optimize for the data distribution at creation. Rising latency, falling relevance, or adding more than 20–30% new data (especially a new domain) signal a rebuild. Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking.

questions.q: A small internal tool can tolerate a short pause in writes at night. You need to rebuild its vector index. Which approach does Learn describe as simpler for this case?

options.text: Switch to an IVFFlat index on an empty table
options.why: IVFFlat needs data to train, and an empty table gives an unusable index.

options.text: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY followed by a rename
options.why: This avoids blocking, but it's the more involved option, meant for systems that can't tolerate downtime.

options.text: Drop the column and reload all embeddings
options.why: That loses data and takes much longer than rebuilding the index.

options.text: REINDEX INDEX during a low-traffic period
options.why: Correct. REINDEX is simpler, but it blocks writes, so schedule it during quiet periods.

questions.hint: Brief interruptions are acceptable here, so you don't need the non-blocking route.
questions.explain: For systems that tolerate brief interruptions, REINDEX INDEX is simpler but blocks writes. For systems that can't, use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, verify, drop the old index, and rename.

questions.q: A legal assistant should return nothing rather than unrelated contracts when no good match exists. What should the query add?

options.text: A threshold: WHERE embedding <=> $1 < 0.4
options.why: Correct. A threshold sets a quality floor; empty results can be the right answer.

options.text: A GIN index on the embedding column
options.why: GIN indexes are for full-text, not vector distance.

options.text: An ORDER BY on created_at instead of distance
options.why: Ordering by date ignores similarity.

options.text: A larger LIMIT, such as LIMIT 100 rows
options.why: A larger LIMIT returns more weak matches.

questions.hint: Returning nothing beats returning something unrelated. Add a cut-off on distance.
questions.explain: Combine a threshold for quality with LIMIT for resource control.

questions.q: An attorney searches for "Smith v. Jones" and expects that exact case name, but vector search returns semantically similar cases first. What should you implement?

options.text: Lower the cosine distance threshold to 0.1
options.why: A stricter threshold may remove results but doesn't match exact names.

options.text: Switch the distance operator from <=> to <->
options.why: Changing the distance metric doesn't add keyword matching.

options.text: Average the query vector with the top result's vector
options.why: Averaging doesn't add exact term matching.

options.text: Hybrid search: vector similarity plus ts_rank
options.why: Correct. Hybrid search captures both semantic and lexical relevance.

questions.hint: Exact names need keyword matching. Combine it with vector similarity.
questions.explain: Use hybrid search for exact terms, names and codes; speed it with a GIN index on the tsvector.

questions.q: A user wants documents about "mergers AND environmental compliance". You have an embedding for each concept. What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Average the two embeddings and run one query
options.why: The average may land near neither concept.

options.text: Query each aspect separately and combine the results
options.why: Correct. Different aspects shouldn't be averaged; retrieve for each and rank by combined relevance.

options.text: Use whichever concept has more documents
options.why: That ignores the other aspect.

options.text: Run the merger query alone, then filter by keyword
options.why: That ignores half the query's meaning.

questions.hint: Two separate concepts are better searched one at a time.
questions.explain: Average only semantically related examples; query distinct aspects separately.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A filtered vector query: `WHERE category = 'contracts' AND practice_area = 'corporate' ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10`.

rows.text: B-tree indexes on category and practice_area can help this query.
Running ANALYZE after loading data helps the planner choose well.
PostgreSQL always uses the vector index, whatever the filter selectivity.
rows.why: With very selective filters, it may scan matching rows without the vector index.

questions.hint: Indexes on filter columns and fresh statistics help the planner.
questions.explain: The planner optimizes total cost; inspect plans with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

questions.q: Match each retrieval metric to what it measures.

items.text: The fraction of retrieved chunks that are actually relevant
items.why: Low precision feeds the LLM irrelevant context.

items.text: The fraction of relevant chunks that were retrieved
How high the first relevant result appears in the list
items.why: Mean Reciprocal Rank rewards early relevant results.

questions.hint: Precision: of what you retrieved, how much was relevant. Recall: of what was relevant, how much did you get. MRR: how soon the first hit appears.
questions.explain: Measure retrieval separately from generation with a labelled evaluation set.

questions.q: Retrieved contract chunks often say "as described above" without containing the referenced text. Which pattern helps?

options.text: Switching to fixed-size chunks with no overlap
options.why: Fixed-size chunks without overlap can cut ideas mid-thought.

options.text: Context-window retrieval of adjacent chunks
options.why: Correct. Fetching neighbours (e.g. 46 and 48 around 47) supplies the missing context.

options.text: Removing the source_documents table entirely
options.why: The source table is needed for citations.

options.text: Lowering the LIMIT to one chunk per query
options.why: Fewer chunks make the missing context worse.

questions.hint: The chunk refers to text that's next to it in the document.
questions.explain: Context windows cost more tokens but reduce incomplete answers.

questions.q: Evaluation shows low recall: answers miss relevant clauses. Which two changes does Learn suggest? (Select two.)

options.text: Increase hnsw.ef_search
options.why: Correct. Higher ef_search searches more candidates and improves recall.

options.text: Tighten the distance threshold
options.why: Tighter thresholds improve precision, not recall.

options.text: Loosen the distance threshold
options.why: Correct. Looser thresholds include more candidates.

options.text: Retrieve fewer chunks per query
options.why: Fewer chunks lower recall.

questions.hint: Low recall: search more widely and accept slightly less similar matches.
questions.explain: Recall levers: looser thresholds, more chunks, higher ef_search or probes.
